content.title: About
content.content: American nonfat cheese is a processed cheese made from skim milk, emulsifiers, salt, and flavorings. It has a smooth, creamy texture, a mild buttery taste, and is commonly used in sandwiches, burgers, and as a topping.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Nonfat American cheese contains less than 0.5% fat.
It is a staple in fast‑food kitchens because it melts quickly and stays stable when heated.
The cheese got its name from the city of Wisconsin, where large‑scale processed cheese production began in the early 1900s.
It often includes added vitamin A and calcium, though in lower amounts than full‑fat cheese.
The low‑fat version is less prone to rancidity, giving it a longer shelf life.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Contains roughly 500 mg of calcium per 100 g, important for bone health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Suitable for low‑fat diets and helps control overall calorie intake.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: The processed nature makes it quick to digest, convenient for sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy proteins or lactose may react to this cheese.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Contains up to 800 mg of salt per 100 g, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Additives and preservatives
items.content: Emulsifiers and flavorings are common and can cause intolerance in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Low vitamin D
items.content: Unlike full‑fat cheese, the nonfat version provides little vitamin D.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice for sandwiches, melt on burgers, stir into omelets, casseroles, and sauces. It melts in seconds in the microwave, making it a quick topping.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 2‑4 °C in the original wrapper or an airtight container. Once opened, use within 2‑3 weeks. Discard if you notice off‑smells, mold, or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn, canned, cooked with oil is a ready‑to‑eat product made from mature corn kernels that are boiled and then sealed in oil. The product retains a sweet flavor and a tender crunch, while the oil adds a subtle richness and extra calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned corn is often used as a quick side dish or an ingredient in salads and soups.
Corn is one of the most widely cultivated vegetables, grown in over 100 countries.
Cooking in oil helps preserve fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin E.
Corn provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.
Several corn varieties are selected for canning, differing in kernel size and sugar content.

items.title: Rich source of carbohydrates
items.content: Corn supplies complex carbs that provide sustained energy.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Lycopene and carotenoids in corn help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Provides magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals contribute to muscle function and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Because of the oil, the product is more caloric than fresh corn, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Canned foods are often salted; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn.

items.title: Bisphenol A in packaging
items.content: If the can is lined with BPA‑containing coating, there may be trace exposure; choose products from reputable brands.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, soups, stews, pasta dishes, or used as a filling for pies. If you want to reduce calories, drain excess oil before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer the corn to an airtight container and keep it refrigerated for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

hot-dog-sandwich-beef-on-wheat-bread.title: Hot dog sandwich, beef, on wheat bread

content.title: About
content.content: A hot dog sandwich with beef on wheat bread is a classic fast‑food item: a juicy beef sausage placed between slices of soft wheat bread, often topped with mustard, ketchup and pickles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first documented hot dog was served in the United States in the late 19th century.
Using wheat bread instead of a traditional bun makes the sandwich softer and milder.
A typical beef sausage contains about 12 % fat, giving it its characteristic flavor and juiciness.
Hot dogs are strongly associated with American sporting events and street festivals.
In some regions the sandwich is finished with cheese sauce or fried onions for extra flavor.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: A beef sausage provides roughly 10 g of protein per serving, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: Wheat bread delivers quick‑acting carbs useful during physical activity.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Sausages are often salty; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Beef sausages contain saturated fats, which may contribute to cardiovascular disease when consumed frequently.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some pre‑made sausages contain nitrites and other preservatives that are best limited in the diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is easy to eat by hand, splitting the bread in half. Add mustard, ketchup, mayo, pickles, onions, cheese or fresh vegetables according to personal taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep sausages refrigerated at +2–4 °C, and the assembled sandwich no longer than 2 hours at room temperature. For longer storage, store bread in an airtight bag and sausages in a separate container.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce, Meat and Vegetables, Ready‑to‑Heat

content.title: About
content.content: This is a ready‑to‑eat meal featuring whole‑grain pasta coated in a tomato‑based sauce, enriched with tender meat and a mix of vegetables. The pasta is pre‑cooked, so it only needs to be heated in a microwave or on the stovetop. The product is designed for a quick, nutritious lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta provides more fiber and micronutrients than refined‑flour pasta.
The tomato sauce is a good source of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Meat in the dish is typically beef or chicken, boosting iron and protein content.
Vegetables such as carrots, broccoli, and bell pepper add vitamins A, C, K, and folate.
The formulation preserves pasta texture and vegetable freshness after heating.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta supplies dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Combined meat and pasta provide a complete set of essential amino acids for tissue repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Tomatoes, vegetables, and whole grains deliver vitamins A, C, K, folate, and iron.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and carotenoids from vegetables help combat free radicals.

items.title: Convenient portion control
items.content: A single ready‑to‑heat package simplifies meal planning and helps avoid overeating.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta contains gluten, so individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose a gluten‑free alternative.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The tomato sauce can be salty; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Ready‑to‑heat meals may contain preservatives for shelf life; those with sensitivities should review the ingredient list.

items.title: Heating guidelines
items.content: Improper heating may lead to uneven temperature and affect flavor and texture.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the portion in the microwave for about 2–3 minutes, stirring halfway to ensure even warming, or heat on the stovetop. Optionally garnish with fresh herbs, grated cheese, or a drizzle of olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store refrigerated at 0–4 °C. See the package for the use‑by date; once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Do not freeze, as this may alter the pasta’s texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Pinto beans are a variety of dry legume popular in Mexican and South American cuisines. White rice is a polished grain that has had its husk and bran removed. Together they form a nutritious, filling dish often used as a side or a base for stews.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “pinto” comes from the Spanish word for “spotted,” referring to the bean’s mottled appearance.
Rice is one of the world’s most consumed foods; more than half of the global population eats rice regularly.
Combining beans and rice provides a complete set of essential amino acids, making the meal a complete protein source.
In traditional Mexican cuisine, pinto beans are commonly served with rice, tomatoes, onions, and spices in a dish called “arroz con frijoles.”
Pinto beans are rich in antioxidants, especially polyphenols, which give them their characteristic color.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Pinto beans contain about 21 g of protein per 100 g dry weight, and rice complements their amino‑acid profile.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in beans supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Provides complex carbohydrates
items.content: White rice offers a quick energy source, while the beans slow the release of carbs for steadier blood sugar.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Both foods are good sources of thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals and trace elements
items.content: Pinto beans supply iron, magnesium and potassium; rice adds phosphorus and modest amounts of zinc.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytates that can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and sprouting lower their levels.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: High glycemic index of rice
items.content: White rice has a high GI, which can raise blood sugar quickly; pairing it with fiber and protein mitigates the effect.

items.title: Food poisoning from undercooking
items.content: Undercooked beans may contain toxic lectins; they should be boiled for at least 10 minutes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook pinto beans and white rice separately until tender, then combine and season with salt, pepper, garlic, onion, or your favorite spices. Use them as a side dish, base for chili, salads, casseroles, or a simple rice‑and‑bean bowl.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 1 year. Cooked beans and rice keep in the refrigerator in a sealed container for 4‑5 days, or freeze in portions for longer storage.
